title: 外部开发的五条黄金法则
content:
The five golden rules of external development | GamesIndustry.biz

We created Code Wizards 24 years ago, and as an external development partner, we work with a mix of small and large companies on backend engineering, live operations, IT and more. Over the years we've learnt from our mistakes, and CEOs of new studios and service providers often ask me how they can best work together for success. Here, I'll share the top five simple rules that you can incorporate into your own playbook to help minimise the stress and maximise the fun of working together.
Golden Rule #1: We're in the business of trust
All games are a piece of art created in a digital form. Trusting somebody to enrich another artist's work is difficult.
Trust is typically built up over the course of years, but working with a new partner requires trust from day one – and that needs an investment.
Any engagement needs to start with an assumption of trust, but we can improve that by continually showing each party is trustworthy. This isn't onerous or difficult, but it does require transparency, planning, and a way of measuring and demonstrating progress. It goes both ways, too: the client is putting their trust in a co-developer or service provider, but the latter also has to trust the client.
The more you build up trust with the client, the more it's likely that any feedback given to them will be listened to
Often the early stages of a game production cycle have largely invisible elements – it's like building a new house, and the foundation takes time, but it is hard to visualise the real effort and work involved. No timesheets will ever be able to demonstrate what's being realised behind the scenes. Find a way of explaining what's going on and ensuring it maps against the agreed plan. Most of all, if you say you'll do something, then do it.
The more you build up trust with the client, the more it's likely that any feedback given to them will be listened to. It's important that all discussion is considered to be valued and well intentioned, and ultimately it will help to make a better game.
Often a prospective new client will message a contact who has worked with us before to find out their opinion of us. A few years ago, I remember taking a call with a potential client who seemed positive but reticent. We closed the discussion on a "maybe." Fifteen minutes later they called back after having spoken to a contact we'd worked with, saying: "They said you're amazing, let's get a contract together." That's the power of reputation and trust.
At all times remember that our industry is a small one – trust is hard to earn and easy to lose. Reputation doubly so. Trust isn't just earned when things are going great, but also when things go wrong. Own your mistakes and fix them. When others make mistakes, jump on and help them get back on track.
TLDR? Treat your reputation like XP – getting to S-Rank is super important.
Golden Rule #2: Flexibility is key
Imagine you're working on a game that everyone is really excited about. Everything is headed in the right direction when all of a sudden, it doesn't feel good enough. What if you encouraged everyone to take a beat and rethink things?
Being able to move things around and change the order that we build them is incredibly important. The key mechanics and functionalities touch every aspect of the game. If it feels like something is off, sharing that feedback immediately is crucial. Strong collaboration and that established trust means that feedback matters and is listened to on all levels.
Games evolve over time, and everybody on the team needs to be willing to bend and flex with them
We're lucky enough to work with a bunch of studios, and there was a great example of the above a decade ago. A renowned studio had a great game, but the wall running just didn't feel right. To get that mechanic working, they needed all of their internal teams pulling together. The pause to fix the issue was two weeks long, which seriously impacted our teams and deliverables – but the game was massively better as a result of the fix (as proved by the Metacritic score). Yes, it caused us a rescheduling nightmare and we had to work harder, but not one member of either team regretted the change.
Games are a form of art and they should be fun, beautiful, and engaging to succeed. One simple detail that feels off can break the experience. That means games evolve over time, and everybody on the team, including service providers, needs to be willing to bend and flex with them, understand how to communicate those changes, and negotiate something that works for all.
Golden Rule #3: Communication is critical
Games teams are a broad church of different kinds of people, from the overtly artistic to those heavily into engineering. They speak slightly different languages, and that needs to be catered to.
In addition communication isn't only written and verbal, it also translates into culture: how the teams fit together and the way they work. Different clients have different ways of operation, and you have to tune into the communication style that works best for them.
The trick is to overcommunicate. You can't assume that everyone knows the project goals, and by overcommunicating, you ensure that everyone involved is part of the same conversation.
Communication style will  change as the game goes on
This is best illustrated in two different examples with two very different communication strategies. For the first team (which is making an epic driving game with a new publisher), we've adopted a "project health" fortnightly reporting cadence. Not only on the deliverables, milestones, and efficacy, but also covering inter-team collaboration, morale boosters and blockers, and ways to improve.
